beats.narration: Twenty-first of May, 2003. Seville. The UEFA Cup final. Celtic against FC Porto, and it has gone to extra time.
Inside the ground, a wall of green and white. Outside it, in the squares and the bars and the streets, thousands more who never had a ticket and came anyway.
How many came? Nobody counted. Every source gives the same estimate: around eighty thousand Celtic supporters, in one city, for one match.

visual.label: Celtic supporters in Seville — an estimate

beats.narration: In the ninety-sixth minute, Bobo Baldé is sent off. Ten men, in extra time, two goals each, and the night still not decided.

Hold that moment there. Because to understand what this night meant to the people in those stands, we have to go back to August 2002, to a summer night in Glasgow, and a defeat that came a fortnight later.
Martin O'Neill's Celtic wanted the Champions League. All that stood in the way was a qualifier against Basel.
At Celtic Park it went to plan. Henrik Larsson in the third minute, Chris Sutton after the break, then Mohamed Sylla late on. Three-one.
A fortnight later, in Switzerland, Basel scored twice and Celtic scored none. Three each on aggregate, and Basel through on the away goal.
So the Champions League was over before September. What was left was the competition nobody had planned the season around. The UEFA Cup.

For the people who had queued for those tickets, it felt like the season had ended before it began. Nobody knew yet that this defeat was the first step of the longest journey the club's supporters had ever made.
It started gently. Sūduva, from Lithuania, came to Glasgow in September and went home beaten eight-one.
Larsson scored three of them in fourteen minutes. Petrov, Sutton, Lambert, Hartson and Valgaeren added the rest.
Two-nil in the return, ten-one on aggregate. Then the draw sent them south of the border, to Blackburn Rovers.
The first leg was tight. One goal, Larsson's, in the eighty-fifth minute.
In England, a fortnight later, Larsson scored again in the fifteenth minute and Sutton finished it. Two-nil away, three-nil overall.
Then Celta Vigo. One-nil at home, Larsson again. In Spain, two goals against, and one for: John Hartson, in the thirty-seventh minute.
Two each on aggregate. In August, the away goal had knocked Celtic out. In December, the away goal put them through.

visual.heading: Away goals
visual.text: Celta Vigo 2–2 on aggregate. Celtic through on away goals.

beats.narration: In the away end in Vigo, those last minutes went on forever. Every Celta attack was a knife. When the whistle went, the Celtic supporters, a long way from home, made a noise you could hear across the ground.
For the first time in a long while, Celtic would play European football after Christmas. The supporters started looking at maps.
February brought Stuttgart. At Celtic Park, Lambert, Shaun Maloney and Stiliyan Petrov. Three-one.
A week later in Germany, Alan Thompson scored in the ninth minute, Sutton two minutes after that. Celtic were cruising.
Then Stuttgart scored three. The night ended three-two to them, and in the away end every one of those minutes felt like an hour. Five-four on aggregate. Through.
The quarter-final draw gave them Liverpool. And what followed was ten days that no Celtic supporter has forgotten.
Thirteenth of March, Celtic Park. Larsson scored in the second minute. Liverpool equalised. One each.
Three days later, the League Cup final at Hampden. Rangers won it, two-one. The mood went from hope to grey in an afternoon.
Four days after that, Anfield. Alan Thompson scored on the stroke of half-time. Then, in the eighty-second minute, John Hartson.
Two-nil at Anfield. Three-one on aggregate. Celtic were in the semi-finals of a European competition, and the away end did not want to go home.
And then, three days later, Inverness Caledonian Thistle knocked them out of the Scottish Cup. One-nil. That was football in March 2003. Glory on Thursday, misery on Sunday.
The semi-final was Boavista, from Porto. At Celtic Park, Larsson scored in the forty-ninth minute. It finished one each.
So everything came down to the second leg, in Portugal. A goalless draw would send Boavista through.
There was a strange twist in that. Boavista and FC Porto share a city. Whoever won in Porto that night would meet a team from Porto in the final.
Seventy-nine minutes went by. Then Larsson. Eleven minutes from the end, he put Celtic into a European final.
One-nil. Two-one on aggregate. The final would be in Seville, on the twenty-first of May, against FC Porto.
What happened next is the part of this story that belongs to the supporters. Within days, Glasgow was trying to get to the south of Spain.
They went by plane, when they could find one. By train, by coach, by car, by ferry, through France, through Portugal, through whatever route was left.
The ground held around fifty-two thousand. Most of the people who made the trip had no ticket, and they knew it before they left.
By the day of the game, Seville belonged to them. The fountains, the plazas, the old streets by the river, all of it green and white, and all of it singing.
UEFA called it the largest travelling support ever assembled for a single game. Around eighty thousand, the estimate says. A city taken over, and not a window broken.

visual.heading: The largest travelling support
visual.text: UEFA's words for the Celtic support in Seville: “the largest travelling support to have assembled for a single game.”

beats.narration: On the other bench sat José Mourinho. Nobody in Seville that night knew yet what that name would come to mean.
Twenty-first of May. Estadio Olímpico de Sevilla. On the stroke of half-time, Derlei put Porto ahead.
Just after the restart, Larsson rose to meet a cross and looped a header over the goalkeeper. One each. It was his two hundredth goal for Celtic.
Within five minutes Porto were ahead again, through Dmitri Alenichev. And in the fifty-seventh minute, Larsson again. Another header. Two each.
Ninety minutes could not separate them. Extra time. And in the ninety-sixth minute, Bobo Baldé was shown a second yellow card.
Ten men held on, and held on. Five minutes from the end of extra time, Derlei scored again.
Celtic two, Porto three, after extra time. The final whistle went in Seville, and eighty thousand people went quiet together.

And then something happened that people still talk about. They stayed. They sang for their team as it walked round the pitch. And the next morning, they started the long way home, having given Seville nothing to complain about.
And there was still a league title to play for. Four days after Seville, on the last day of the season, Celtic and Rangers were level on points and level on goal difference.
Celtic, with tired legs, won four-nil at Kilmarnock. At Ibrox, Rangers beat Dunfermline six-one.
Ninety-seven points each. Rangers champions by a single goal of goal difference. The closest finish the league had ever seen.
A European final lost in extra time. A league lost by one goal. Four days apart. On paper, Celtic ended that season with nothing.
But that is not how the people who went to Seville remember it.
That year, FIFA gave its Fair Play Award to Celtic's supporters, for the way they behaved in Seville. UEFA honoured them too, at Celtic Park the following season.

visual.heading: FIFA Fair Play Award 2003
visual.text: Awarded to Celtic's supporters, for their behaviour at the 2003 UEFA Cup final.

beats.narration: Henrik Larsson finished the season with forty-four goals. Ten of them came in that UEFA Cup run, two of them in the final.
Seven ties, from a Lithuanian town to Anfield to Porto. The road is still told in pubs in Glasgow, round by round, as if it happened last week.
They lost the final. They lost the league. And they came home with a story they have told ever since. Football is ninety minutes. Being a supporter is a lifetime.
end

description:
In 2002–03, Celtic were knocked out of the Champions League in August and ended the season with nothing on paper: a UEFA Cup final lost to FC Porto after extra time in Seville on 21 May, and a league title lost to Rangers by one goal of goal difference four days later.

This film follows the whole road from the stands, in order: Basel in August, Sūduva, Blackburn Rovers, Celta Vigo, Stuttgart, the ten days in March around Liverpool, the semi-final against Boavista, and the journey of an estimated 80,000 supporters to Seville — the support that won FIFA's Fair Play Award that year.

Every score, date and table on screen is printed from FanLife's archive records (UEFA match records) and the sources listed below. The crowd in Seville is an estimate in every source and the film says so.
